summary: Uganda Trend Detective is an interactive tool that detects and tests climate trends across Uganda using NASA data. Users pick a variable (rainfall or temperature), a season and a time period. The app plots the time series, runs a Mann-Kendall trend test with Sen’s slope, and reports whether the change is statistically significant. An interactive map of 16 locations shows where trends are occurring, with a correction for testing many locations at once. A satellite cross-check compares NASA POWER (MERRA-2 reanalysis) with GPM IMERG satellite rainfall to test whether findings hold across independent datasets. For Kampala’s second rainy season, POWER shows a significant increase that the satellite data does not confirm, and the tool reports this as uncertain instead of overclaiming. Data: NASA POWER and GPM IMERG via NASA Giovanni.
details:
Project Overview: Uganda Trend Detective

What does it do and how does it work?Uganda Trend Detective is an interactive climate and Earth-system analysis web application built by team PnP for the Be an Earth System Trend Detective challenge. It helps users distinguish real, statistically significant environmental shifts in Uganda from natural year-to-year climate variability ("noise").

Users select a climate variable (such as rainfall), a specific season (e.g., Uganda's second rainy season), and a multi-decade time period. The application automatically queries NASA Earth observation datasets across 16 key locations in Uganda and runs statistical trend analyses on each site:

  1. Interactive Map & Multiple-Testing Correction: Each location is plotted with color coding for trend magnitude and visual indicators (glowing vs. faded markers) for statistical significance. Crucially, the tool applies multiple-hypothesis testing corrections across all 16 locations simultaneously showing both how many sites initially appear significant ([X] of 16) and how many remain robust after correcting for false positives ([Y] of 16).
  2. Location Drill-Down & Detective Reports: Clicking any site reveals its historical time series, decadal trend rate,p-value, a plain-language verdict, and a downloadable summary "detective report."
  3. Satellite Cross-Check Engine: To prevent single-dataset bias, the app cross-checks model-based reanalysis data (NASA POWER) against independent gauge-calibrated satellite observations (GPM IMERG). When two datasets correlate year-to-year (e.g., r=0.69r=0.69 in Kampala) but disagree on the long-term trend slope and statistical significance, the app explicitly flags the result as "Not confirmed, uncertain."

What benefits does it have, and what is the intended impact? Farmers, water-resource managers, and regional planners in Uganda depend on accurate long-term rainfall and climate trends to make high-stakes decisions around planting seasons, crop selection, and infrastructure. Relying on a single climate dataset or mistaking random weather noise for a permanent shift can lead to costly miscalculations.

Our intended impact is to democratize rigorous climate statistics. By translating p-values, multiple-testing adjustments ,and multi-satellite cross-validation into clear visual cues and plain-language verdicts, Uganda Trend Detective empowers local decision-makers and educators to act with confidence when trends are real and exercise caution when the data is uncertain.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Data Sources: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) API and NASA GPM IMERG (Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM) satellite precipitation data.
  • Languages & Frameworks:  Python (Pandas, SciPy/Statsmodels, Requests) for statistical analysis and API pipelines; Streamlit / React / Leaflet / Plotly for the interactive web dashboard and mapping.
  • Development Tools: Git/GitHub for version control, VS Code, Jupyter Notebooks for prototyping statistical test.

How is your project creative? Most hackathon climate dashboards focus on visualizing raw data or highlighting the most dramatic upward/downward slopes. We took the opposite, "detective" approach: building scientific skepticism directly into the user interface. Instead of presenting every trend line as absolute truth, we gamified and humanized rigorous statistical concepts—turning p-values, Bonferroni/FDR multiple-testing corrections, and inter-dataset divergence into intuitive visual signals (glowing vs. faded markers) and an honest "Uncertain" verdict banner.

What factors did your team consider?

  • False Positives Across Space: Testing 16 locations at once increases the statistical likelihood of finding a "significant" trend purely by chance. We specifically accounted for multiple-testing bias so users aren't misled by isolated anomalies.
  • Dataset Divergence: Reanalysis models (POWER) and satellite-gauge products (GPM IMERG) measure and model precipitation differently. Comparing them over an identical 24-year baseline ensured fair apples-to-apples validation.
  • Accessibility & Actionability: Complex statistical outputs mean little to non-specialists. We designed plain-language verdicts and downloadable one-page detective reports so findings can be easily shared outside the app.
